chunks: And Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Minqarī narrated from Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyāth, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
A man said to him: “Tell me, if I see something in a man’s hands, is it permissible for me to testify that it belongs to him?” He said: “Yes.”

I said: “But perhaps it belongs to someone else.” He said: “Then from where is it permissible for you to buy it, and it becomes your property, then after ownership you say, ‘It is mine,’ and swear upon it, yet it is not permissible for you to ascribe it to the one from whom its ownership came to you?”
Then Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “If this were not permissible, no marketplace for the Muslims would stand.”

key_terms.أَشْهَدَ: to testify or bear witness regarding ownership
key_terms.تَحْلِفَ: to swear an oath in support of a claim
key_terms.تَشْتَرِيَهُ: to purchase it in a legally recognized transaction
key_terms.تَنْسُبَهُ: to attribute or ascribe ownership to someone
key_terms.فِي يَدَيْ رَجُلٍ: in the possession or control of a man

ai.seo_question: Can a person testify that an item belongs to the one who possesses it?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes that outward possession is a valid basis for attributing ownership in testimony and transactions. Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام explains that ordinary buying, selling, and claiming ownership would become impossible if possession were not legally recognized. The report supports practical legal order in Muslim commercial life.
